title: Band structure of two-dimensional graphene and of one-dimensional nanoribbons via variational quantum algorithms: from energies to wavefunction quality
authors: Raúl Medrano Millán, Rodrigo Gil-Merino y Rubio, Juan Borge, Unai Aseguinolaza Aguirreche
abstract: Simulating quantum many-body systems classically encounters exponential bottlenecks, which quantum devices circumvent by natively encoding wavefunctions. In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, however, hardware noise constrains simulation accuracy. As a stepping stone toward strongly correlated materials, we compute the band structure of 2D monolayer graphene and 1D nanoribbons (zigzag and armchair) using a single variational workflow in the $p_z$ tight-binding approximation. Non-interacting ground states also provide essential initial reference states for subspace and warm-started variational methods to solve interacting spectra. By mapping the Bloch Hamiltonian to Pauli operators, we extract the ground band via the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and excited subbands via Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD), validating our approach from ideal simulations to execution on physical IBM Quantum processors. In ideal simulations, the workflow reproduces exact diagonalization results with high precision, whereas hardware noise introduces energy deviations of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter. While qubit counts scale logarithmically with ribbon width, fixed-depth ansatz accuracy degrades with Hilbert space dimension. Crucially, deepening the ansatz improves ideal simulation accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but worsens energy estimates under noise, proving that practical circuit depth is bounded by hardware noise rather than expressivity. Finally, we complement energy evaluations with a wavefunction-level diagnostic measuring subspace containment. This diagnostic captures degenerate manifolds and exposes optimization failure modes disguised by energy agreement alone. Operating directly on NISQ hardware, this validated workflow establishes a controlled baseline for studying topological and strongly correlated phases in realistic materials.

infographic.key_insight: Variational quantum algorithms reproduce graphene and nanoribbon band structures, but hardware noise limits useful circuit depth and energy agreement alone can mask wavefunction errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow provides a validated NISQ baseline and non-interacting reference states for future simulations of correlated materials.
method: Map graphene and nanoribbon Bloch Hamiltonians in the p_z tight-binding approximation to Pauli operators.
Use VQE for the ground band and VQD for excited subbands.
Validate against exact diagonalization and assess wavefunctions with a subspace-containment diagnostic.
infographic.evidence_signal: Ideal simulations closely match exact diagonalization; deeper ansatz circuits improve ideal accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but worsen noisy energy estimates, with hardware deviations of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter.
infographic.watch_item: Logarithmic qubit scaling with ribbon width does not ensure accuracy: fixed-depth ansatz performance degrades as the Hilbert space grows.
infographic.paper_title: Band structure of two-dimensional graphene and of one-dimensional nanoribbons via variational quantum algorithms: from energies to wavefunction quality

title: Runtime Compilation for Quantum Circuits with PQF-Enabled $R_z$ Synthesis
authors: Siddharth Dangwal, Christopher Kang, Jad Habhab, Ritvik Sharma, Frederic T. Chong, Gokul Subramanian Ravi
abstract: In Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) using surface codes, reducing $T$-count is critical for efficient computation due to the high cost of $T$-state distillation. Probabilistic Quantum Circuit with Fallback (PQF) synthesis significantly lowers $T$-counts compared to standard protocols like Gridsynth, but introduces high circuit dynamism through extra gates inserted at runtime. This dynamism invalidates static compile-time routing, as these new $T$ gates require dynamic lattice surgery routing to establish non-intersecting ancilla paths to $T$-state factories while minimizing total execution time. To address this, we introduce $\text{R}^2$-PQF, a Runtime Routing protocol for PQF-synthesized quantum circuits. $\text{R}^2$-PQF dynamically routes gates layer-by-layer, computing paths during the execution of the previous logical timestep. To satisfy the strict computational window of $\sim t_{lattice\_surgery} + t_{reaction}$ and non-intersectionality constraints, we implement a Wavefront Breadth-First Search (W-BFS) and synthesise it on a 500MHz FPGA and 2 GHz ASIC. For a clock cycle of 2GHz, we achieve a median logical time-step of $1.51 μs$ for a 300 qubit Ising Hamiltonian circuit, demonstrating that $\text{R}^2$-PQF successfully resolves the vast majority of paths (with rare exceptions) within the execution window and enables the $T$-count benefits of PQF without latency penalties. Compared to a baseline stalling-based solution (the only no-runtime-recomputation solution), $\text{R}^2$-PQF speeds up circuit execution by $1.34\times$ on average and up to $1.76 \times$.

infographic.key_insight: R²-PQF enables lower-T-count PQF quantum circuits by routing runtime-inserted gates fast enough to avoid latency penalties in most cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-accelerated runtime routing can help surface-code quantum computers exploit PQF synthesis despite unpredictable T-state delivery paths.
method: Route gates layer by layer while the previous logical timestep executes.
Use Wavefront Breadth-First Search to find non-intersecting lattice-surgery paths to T-state factories.
Implement the router on a 500 MHz FPGA and a 2 GHz ASIC.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 1.51 μs median logical timestep for a 300-qubit Ising Hamiltonian circuit at 2 GHz, with execution speedups averaging 1.34× and reaching 1.76× over a stalling-based baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Rare routing-window overruns remain, so median timing does not guarantee stall-free execution for every layer or workload.
infographic.paper_title: Runtime Compilation for Quantum Circuits with PQF-Enabled $R_z$ Synthesis

title: On Revolutionizing Power Systems: Suitability of Quantum Computing-Ready Pipelines for Stochastic Unit Commitment Optimization
authors: Ying-Yi Hong, Dylan Josh Domingo Lopez
abstract: Modern unit commitment (UC) scenarios, particularly those involving uncertainties from demand fluctuations and renewable energy sources, pose significant challenges to traditional optimization methods due to the large search spaces they encompass. This paper proposes a quantum computing-ready optimization pipeline for deterministic and stochastic UC, integrating classical, quantum-inspired, quantum annealing, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers across test systems, including the IEEE 118-bus system. A novel Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) reformulation accommodates generator scaling and 24-hour scheduling horizons with compact Boolean logic penalties for startup, cooldown, and spinning reserve constraints. A divide-and-conquer strategy and Quantum Computing Monte Carlo (QCMC) simulation address scalability across 27,730 uncertainty scenarios, reducing compilation time by up to two orders of magnitude. Experimental results demonstrate the pipeline's ability to achieve efficient, scalable, and accurate UC optimization under uncertainty: the hybrid quantum method approach matches the classical baseline, reduces stochastic UC runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours, and characterizes pure quantum annealing as limited to small systems with 0.22% to 2.18% encoding errors and constraint violations. These results provide an analysis of the scalability and computational practicality of hybrid quantum optimization for generator scheduling in UC.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum-ready unit commitment pipeline matches the classical baseline with a hybrid solver while reducing reported stochastic scheduling runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline offers a practical route to evaluating hybrid quantum optimization for generator scheduling under demand and renewable-energy uncertainty.
method: Encode 24-hour generator schedules as QUBO problems with compact penalties for startup, cooldown, and spinning reserve constraints.
Integrate classical, quantum-inspired, quantum annealing, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers.
Use divide-and-conquer and Quantum Computing Monte Carlo simulation to handle uncertainty scenarios.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation includes the IEEE 118-bus system and 27,730 uncertainty scenarios, with compilation time reduced by up to two orders of magnitude.
infographic.watch_item: Pure quantum annealing remains limited to small systems, with reported encoding errors of 0.22%–2.18% and constraint violations.
infographic.paper_title: On Revolutionizing Power Systems: Suitability of Quantum Computing-Ready Pipelines for Stochastic Unit Commitment Optimization

title: Hybrid Quantum--Classical Pauli-Correlator Architecture for Image Reconstruction
authors: Sparsho Chakraborty, Siddhartha Patra
abstract: We introduce the Pauli-Correlator Autoencoder (PCAE), a hybrid quantum--classical architecture for image reconstruction. PCAE splits an image into patches and compresses each patch as a matrix product state (MPS). A small quantum circuit turns each compressed patch into a few measured numbers, and a classical neural network rebuilds the patch from these numbers and the patch position. A learnable energy term, taken from physics, is added to training and tracked as training proceeds. Two versions place the six qubits on a line (PCAE1D) or on a grid (PCAE2D). An averaging step makes the PCAE2D features follow rotations and reflections of the image exactly. Trained on one image at a time, PCAE2D rebuilds images from six public datasets with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 25.8 to 41.6 decibels. On CIFAR-10 images not used in training, a formula-based stand-in for the PCAE2D features performs within 1 decibel of several simpler classical methods. Five trained models also run on real IBM quantum computers without retraining, and rebuild images at 25.90 to 31.52 decibels. A short argument and a synthetic test show that, with a linear final layer, measuring qubits in pairs is needed for targets built from products of inputs. These results show that PCAE works as a hybrid model that rebuilds varied images and runs on today's quantum hardware at the six-qubit scale.

infographic.key_insight: A six-qubit hybrid quantum–classical autoencoder reconstructs images using measured Pauli correlators and a classical neural decoder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture runs on current IBM quantum hardware without retraining, demonstrating a small-scale implementation rather than quantum advantage.
method: Split images into patches and compress each patch as a matrix product state.
Extract quantum features with six qubits arranged in a line or grid, then decode using features and patch position.
Train with a learnable physics-inspired energy term; average grid-model features for exact rotation/reflection equivariance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained per image across six public datasets, PCAE2D achieved 25.8–41.6 dB PSNR; five trained models achieved 25.90–31.52 dB on IBM hardware without retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization evidence uses a formula-based feature surrogate on unseen CIFAR-10 images, so it does not establish end-to-end quantum generalization or advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Hybrid Quantum--Classical Pauli-Correlator Architecture for Image Reconstruction

title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Alejandro Mayorga-Redondo, José Daniel Viqueira, Diego Alvarez-Estevez, Eduardo Mosqueira-Rey, Andrés Gómez
abstract: This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum recurrent model detected apneic versus normal breathing with performance comparable to classical recurrent models while using far fewer parameters and few qubits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact quantum recurrent architectures warrant investigation for physiological time-series classification, though these results do not establish a practical quantum advantage.
method: Use a variational classical–quantum recurrent architecture.
Classify breathing time series as apneic or normal.
Compare against classical recurrent neural networks.

infographic.paper_title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks

title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding for Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization
authors: Samuele Cavinato, Marco Tesoro, Gianluca Morettini, Marta Paiusco, Alessandro Scaggion, Simone Montangero
abstract: Optimizing continuous-variable functions on qubit-based quantum hardware requires a finite representation of the search space and a solver-compatible representation of the objective function. Fixed-grid discretizations provide a direct encoding, but restrict the search to a predefined range and resolution; at the same time, constructing a compact Hamiltonian for a general continuous-variable objective can be impractical. Here, we introduce a framework for continuous-variable optimization tailored to qubit-based quantum architectures. The method combines an adaptive discretization with an iterative local mapping of the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian. We assess the approach on unconstrained and constrained instances of the $n$-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmark, and on a proof-of-concept inverse-planning problem in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for cancer treatment. The results show that this framework can produce competitive solutions, supporting its use as a flexible mapping strategy for continuous-variable optimization in qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive discretization and iterative local spin-glass mappings enable continuous-variable optimization on qubit-based architectures without a fixed search grid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a flexible way to translate continuous engineering objectives into solver-compatible problems for quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines.
method: Adapt the finite encoding of continuous variables during optimization.
Iteratively map the objective locally onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian.
Solve the mapped problems within a qubit-compatible optimization pipeline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on unconstrained and constrained n-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmarks and a proof-of-concept radiotherapy inverse-planning problem yielded competitive solutions, according to the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify scaling, mapping overhead, or advantage over classical solvers, leaving practical performance uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding for Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization

title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics
authors: Shao-Bo Zhou, Yu-Ze Zhu, Hang Song, Xiang Zhao, Lin Yang, Xian-Min Jin
abstract: Neural networks that predict chaotic dynamics can reproduce short trajectories while misrepresenting statistics over long times. Quantum priors represent selected dynamical statistics through quantum generative models and provide statistical constraints for classical neural networks. Training a separate prior for each value of a system parameter, such as the Reynolds number, does not explicitly model how these statistics vary with that parameter. We learn a conditional quantum prior that approximates selected statistics of an invariant measure at unseen parameter values within the training range, without retraining. For Lorenz-63, the prior reduces mean Jensen-Shannon divergence by 56.9% relative to a classical multilayer perceptron with a comparable number of weights across 96 unseen parameter values. Across 101 values of the same parameter, the shared prior uses 84.7% fewer trainable weights than would be required by a separate quantum neural network at each value. We then use the learned prior to regularize classical neural networks, encouraging their autoregressive rollouts to better reproduce long-term statistics. For Kolmogorov flow at Reynolds number $Re=1000$, prior regularization reduces forecast mean squared error by 66.0% over 318 steps relative to the classical baseline without prior regularization. We also implement a photonic quantum prior for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, achieving a mean Jensen-Shannon divergence of $4.58\times10^{-3}$ for Lorenz-63 and $2.59\times10^{-3}$ for Kolmogorov flow at unseen parameter values.

infographic.key_insight: A conditional quantum prior learns how selected chaotic-system statistics vary with a parameter, generalizing to unseen values within the training range without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Regularizing classical predictors with this prior can improve long-term statistical fidelity and forecast accuracy while sharing trainable weights across parameter values.
method: Train a parameter-conditioned quantum generative model on selected invariant-measure statistics.
Use the learned prior to regularize classical neural-network autoregressive rollouts.
Implement a photonic quantum prior for NISQ devices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 56.9% lower mean Jensen–Shannon divergence than a comparably sized MLP across 96 unseen Lorenz-63 parameter values, 84.7% fewer weights than separate quantum models across 101 values, and 66.0% lower forecast MSE over 318 Kolmogorov-flow steps at Re=1000.
infographic.watch_item: Results establish interpolation within the training parameter range, not extrapolation or computational speedup over classical methods.
infographic.paper_title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics

title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
authors: Arpit Arora, Adam Holmes, Krysta M. Svore, Taylor L. Patti
abstract: Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model. Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics. An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-agent-assisted, Lean-verified pipeline checks whether a quantum device’s effective Hamiltonian preserves the intended topological code’s low-energy subspace.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow identifies viable device parameters and dominant unwanted interactions to guide coupling and control improvements for analog quantum error correction.
method: Construct the ideal code Hamiltonian and determine its protective excitation gap.
Check low-energy state isolation and subspace agreement using Lean.
Compare unwanted energy-shift bounds from interaction-strength sums, anticommuting Pauli grouping, and diagonalization.

infographic.watch_item: The guarantees concern an effective device model; robustness to experimental noise, model mismatch, and larger arrays remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware

title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs
authors: Dongwhee Kim, Suhas Vittal, Poulami Das
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers run millions of logical cycles to perform quantum error correction (QEC). As logical operations span entire logical cycles, the logical cycle time (LCT) dictates program runtime. Qubit measurements, critical to extract parity information for QEC, are the slowest operations and account for 43-86% of LCT. Measurement latencies impact fidelity: fast measurements lower our ability to correctly classify quantum states, whereas slow measurements increase the likelihood of decoherence. Hardware providers thus calibrate measurement latencies that maximize readout fidelity per qubit and use them to schedule all measurements during program execution. However, calibrated latencies are sub-optimal for logical performance because logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds, during which data qubits are not measured. This increases LCT and logical error rates (LERs) due to decoherence at the logical level. We propose DynaMite, a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy built on two key insights. First, logical cycles must use a measurement latency that is fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code, instead of the calibrated latency that only maximizes readout fidelity. Second, not all logical cycles are equal; many do not fully utilize the error budget of the QEC code, i.e., the number of failed parity checks it can tolerate without compromising LER. These cycles could use even faster measurements but do not, because latencies are chosen statically, whereas error information is only available at runtime. DynaMite exploits the fact that a logical cycle comprises multiple QEC rounds and selects the fastest latency for an upcoming round based on the error budget left and rounds remaining. Our evaluations show that DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69x on average and up to 2.29x, and reduces LER to 0.46x on average and up to 0.13x of baseline.

infographic.key_insight: Dynamically selecting measurement latency from the remaining error budget and QEC rounds can shorten logical cycles while reducing logical errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing measurements for logical performance rather than per-qubit readout fidelity can accelerate fault-tolerant quantum programs.
method: Use measurement latencies that balance logical cycle time and logical error rate.
Track the remaining error budget and QEC rounds within each logical cycle.
Select the fastest suitable latency for the upcoming round using a lightweight real-time policy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations report 1.69× average logical-cycle speedup, reaching 2.29×, with logical error rates averaging 0.46× baseline and reaching as low as 0.13×.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires timely runtime error information and measurement-latency control; the abstract does not specify hardware validation or controller overhead.
infographic.paper_title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs

title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit
authors: Giovanni Adriano, Akilan Rajamani, Francesco Hoch, Farrokh Labib, Nadja Z. Zaouri, Eugenio Caruccio
abstract: Quantum simulations of molecular electronic structure hold the potential for computational advantage but are inherently limited by the linear scaling of qubit requirements with respect to system size. Quantum Density Functional Theory (Q-DFT) addresses this constraint by reformulating the interacting many-body problem in terms of a non-interacting Kohn--Sham reference system. Here, we present and experimentally validate a Q-DFT algorithm that requires only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2(N))$ qubits to simulate a system of $N$ orbitals, thereby reducing resource overhead. More precisely, we solve the Kohn--Sham problem for the lithium hydride (LiH) molecule using the ensemble extension of the variational quantum eigensolver paradigm that minimizes the energy of the system in the subspace spanned by the ground and first excited states. To execute this task, we encode the problem with qubits on a quantum photonic platform, utilizing an architecture that combines a deterministic quantum dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated photonic circuit. By evaluating the molecular ground- and first excited-state properties, this work establishes a pathway for simulating larger molecular systems, demonstrating the viability of integrating qubit-efficient algorithms with advanced reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry applications.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Density Functional Theory reduces qubit requirements to O(log₂ N) for N orbitals by solving a non-interacting Kohn–Sham reference problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pairing qubit-efficient algorithms with programmable photonic hardware offers a route toward near-term molecular simulation with reduced qubit overhead.
method: Reformulate electronic structure using a non-interacting Kohn–Sham reference system.
Use ensemble variational quantum eigensolving to minimize energy in a ground- and first-excited-state subspace.
Encode qubits on a photonic platform combining a deterministic quantum-dot single-photon source and a programmable integrated circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental validation on lithium hydride (LiH), evaluating molecular ground- and first-excited-state properties without providing numerical accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Logarithmic qubit scaling does not establish total computational advantage; larger-system performance and accuracy remain to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit

title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform
authors: Sharyu Kekane, Sadique Khatib, Abhushan Bokade, Uday Wad, S. M. Kamalapur, Y. D. Bhise
abstract: Most quantum circuit platforms focus on idealized circuit assembly and simulation, hiding hardware compilation, error identification, and variational model training behind black-box operations. QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification. Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits. This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond. The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17. Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. The router introduces approximately 1.27x more SWAP gates than Qiskit's SABRE due to its omission of optimization, trading routing efficiency for complete decision transparency and traceability.

infographic.key_insight: QYANTRAM makes quantum compilation, verification, error identification, and model training transparent and independently checkable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Traceable compilation and exact active-qubit verification help engineers audit quantum workflows on large hardware layouts.
method: Expose compilation stages, routing scores, and rejected SWAP candidates.
Verify only k active qubits when inactive qubits remain in |0>, reducing state-space complexity from 2^N to 2^k.
Exhaustively evaluate Pauli error patterns and validate model-training numerics against Qiskit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports sub-millisecond pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts with approximately 10,000× speed-ups, error predictions agreeing within 2.8e-17, and training 25–50× faster with numerical agreement within 2.0e-15.
infographic.watch_item: Routing omits optimization and uses approximately 1.27× as many SWAP gates as Qiskit's SABRE, trading efficiency for transparency.
infographic.paper_title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform

title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
authors: Yuxuan Du, Hanqing Zhao, Xinbiao Wang, Yiming Lu, Kaining Zhang, Dacheng Tao
abstract: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.

infographic.key_insight: AI scientists struggle to reproduce quantum research from papers alone, but externally verified workflow repairs can become reusable experience that improves performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Verified, reusable workflows could make computational quantum research automation more reliable and cost-effective without changing the underlying model.
method: Build OmniQ, an expert-audited environment that turns published studies into executable reproduction tasks.
Use Residual Agents to distil externally verified workflow repairs into reusable research experience.

infographic.paper_title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists

title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Manav Seksaria, Advith Desu, Anil Prabhakar
abstract: Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over ansatze and depths, and training each candidate. We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training. First, a circuit without entangling gates has a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every subset of qubits. A singular value decomposition of a dataset's Fourier coefficients therefore indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits it connects, and a lower bound on the error of omitting it. Second, the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix grows by $p_0$ per layer, after a first-layer deficit $d_0$, until it reaches a ceiling set by the dynamical Lie algebra. This law fixes the depth. Third, reading out all $2^N - 1$ Pauli-Z products from one batch of shots resolves half of the state's directions, the most any single-basis readout can. A single-qubit readout resolves an exponentially small fraction. For the Madelon dataset, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Three data- and gate-informed rules select entanglement structure, circuit depth and readout for variational quantum circuits before training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach replaces ansatz-and-depth grid searches with principled design choices, potentially reducing quantum model development costs.
method: Use dataset Fourier-coefficient SVDs to identify needed entanglement and bound the error from omitting it.
Set depth using quantum Fisher information rank growth and its dynamical Lie algebra ceiling.
Estimate all 2^N − 1 Pauli-Z products from one shot batch to maximize directions resolved by single-basis readout.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Madelon, the rules selected seven three-qubit blocks at depth three, yielding a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy without grid search; ablations showed lower accuracy with shallower circuits, smaller blocks or no reuploading.
infographic.watch_item: Although all Pauli-Z products share a measurement basis, their exponentially growing number raises classical processing and finite-shot precision concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits

title: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization
authors: Adam Husted Kjelstrøm, Jaco van de Pol, Andreas Pavlogiannis
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is an indispensable component of the quantum software stack, used to reduce noise, maximize performance, alleviate costs of quantum error correction, or target specific hardware. A related problem is approximate membership: for a fixed set of unitaries $S$, decide whether a given circuit $C$ is within distance $\varepsilon$ of a unitary in $S$ under some metric $m$. Membership is a special case of optimization, where $S$ is a set of unitaries implementable at no cost (e.g., with noise-minimal circuits, or without magic states). Janzing, Wocjan, and Beth (Int. J. Quantum Inf., 2005) showed that, for the operator metric, the case $S=\{I\}$ (approximate identity) is QMA-complete when $C$ is promised to be either close to the identity or far from it. We generalize this setting in three directions: (i) promise-free inputs, (ii) besides $S=\{I\}$, sets $S$ containing only Clifford unitaries, or only generalized permutation matrices (i.e., no superposition), and (iii) the trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics. We show that, in all cases, approximate membership is PP-hard for wide ranges of $\varepsilon$, provided $C$'s gate-set can implement Clifford+T, as the gate-sets of standard hardware do. If $S=\{I\}$, or if $S$ contains only generalized permutation matrices, $I\in S$, and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds for all non-trivial $\varepsilon$. If $S=\{I\}$ and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds even for circuits over classical-reversible gate-sets. Our results indicate that approximate membership is harder over promise-free inputs than the QMA-complete promise version, and that this hardness persists across quantum resources (any gates, non-Clifford, superposition) and distance metrics. They directly imply PP-hardness of circuit optimization when minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth or count.

infographic.key_insight: Without input promises, approximate quantum circuit membership is PP-hard across multiple target-unitary sets and distance metrics, implying PP-hardness of related circuit optimization tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results establish worst-case barriers to minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate count and depth on hardware supporting Clifford+T.
method: Analyze promise-free membership near the identity, Clifford-only sets, and generalized-permutation-only sets.
Establish PP-hardness under trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics across wide approximation ranges.
Derive hardness consequences for circuit optimization, including selected cases using classical-reversible gates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical hardness results rather than empirical benchmarks, with PP-hardness for all non-trivial tolerances in specified trace-based cases.
infographic.watch_item: These are worst-case complexity results; they do not establish that practical heuristics or structured circuit instances are uniformly difficult.
infographic.paper_title: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization

title: Initialization-controlled fault sensitivity and force-balance plateaus in noisy variational quantum optimization
authors: Longhui Shen, Fangzhou Jin, Bin Guo
abstract: We study deep variational circuits for a periodic Heisenberg chain under local gate depolarization, at depths where noiseless training is coherently exact. Full-width initializations reach low coherent error faster than circuits with confined transverse generators, but incur a larger noise shift and need an order of magnitude more updates for noisy convergence. In many-body-localization-inspired initialization, bounding the initial transverse generator amplitudes keeps the operator support localized and suffices for low-fragility optimization, so longitudinal disorder and Floquet layer repetition are unnecessary. The fault-erasure fraction, the mean fraction of coherent energy removed per fault, sets the effective visibility through a parameter-free exponential model. Full-width circuits start with delocalized operator support, and once coherent energy builds up, each fault erases nearly all of it. Initially, their noise-induced gradient almost uniformly attenuates the coherent gradient, so coherent descent proceeds at the noiseless rate. They then stall on a high-noise force-balance plateau, where finite coherent and noise-induced gradients cancel to first order. At late times all initializations reach the same fault-erasure fraction and noisy-error band, but operator support contracts more slowly, at a rate set by the plateau residence time.

infographic.key_insight: Bounding initial transverse generator amplitudes reduces noise fragility, while full-width initialization learns faster coherently but stalls on plateaus where coherent and noise-induced gradients cancel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Initialization offers a practical lever for reducing noisy optimization cost without requiring longitudinal disorder or repeated Floquet layers.
method: Study deep variational circuits for a periodic Heisenberg chain under local gate depolarization.
Compare full-width initialization with confined transverse-generator initialization.
Relate fault-erasure fraction to effective visibility using a parameter-free exponential model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Full-width circuits require roughly an order of magnitude more updates for noisy convergence, although all tested initializations eventually reach the same fault-erasure fraction and noisy-error band.
infographic.watch_item: The findings concern a specific spin-chain setting and local depolarizing noise; transfer to hardware noise and other circuit architectures needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Initialization-controlled fault sensitivity and force-balance plateaus in noisy variational quantum optimization

title: High-fidelity quantum gate learning via physics-informed neural networks
authors: Luis Fabra, Cristian E. Susa, Alcides Montoya, Ariel Norambuena
abstract: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of $8.49\times10^{-8}$ for Hadamard and values between $3.39\times10^{-7}$ and $4.96\times10^{-6}$ for controlled-NOT under $XX$, $YY$, and $ZZ$ interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of $K_\ast=24$ coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below $10^{-6}$. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at $K=30$ preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity $10^{-5}$ at $N=128$ and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed neural networks learn smooth controls for high-fidelity one- and two-qubit gates while enabling compact control representations and square-pulse playback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach connects accurate gate synthesis with control-resource choices and discretized pulse execution relevant to quantum hardware.
method: Train with Schrödinger dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization, and multiple initial states from mutually unbiased bases.
Validate using Haar-random input states and average gate fidelity; test dephasing and amplitude damping with Lindblad dynamics.
Compress controls using boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions and evaluate square-pulse playback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Unitary simulations achieved average infidelity of 8.49×10⁻⁸ for Hadamard and 3.39×10⁻⁷–4.96×10⁻⁶ for CNOT; at K=30, square-pulse and Strang propagation preserved all 31 polynomial references within 10⁻⁵ infidelity at N≥128 tested resolutions.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based; experimental performance remains to be established under hardware calibration errors, bandwidth limits, and noise beyond the modeled dissipation.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity quantum gate learning via physics-informed neural networks

title: Entanglement-Aware Quantum Circuit Optimization through Globally Optimal Partitioning
authors: Gregory Morse, Muhammad Al Farizi, Jakab Nádori, László Hajas, Tamás Kozsik, Peter Rakyta
abstract: We introduce a scalable framework for globally optimal quantum-circuit partitioning and entanglement-aware block resynthesis. The partitioning problem is formulated as an integer linear program over qubit-feasible convex subcircuits, supporting objectives such as minimizing the number of partitions or a weighted execution cost. The resulting partition selection is exact over the enumerated feasible candidates and their computed costs when the ILP is solved to proven optimality. The selected partitions are resynthesized using an operator-Schmidt rank (OSR) based synthesis technique, which exploits their internal entanglement structure. We compare the end-to-end integer linear programming (ILP)--OSR workflow with BQSKit while identifying their different routing methods, and separately compare local OSR and BQSKit synthesis on matched three- and four-qubit unitaries. On the frozen sample of 772 local unitary targets, OSR produces 741 verified syntheses versus 617 for BQSKit, and matches or improves the CNOT count in all 617 jointly verified pairs. These results demonstrate that globally optimal partition selection combined with entanglement-aware resynthesis improves circuit quality and extends block-based optimization to problem sizes that are impractical for existing optimization workflows.

infographic.key_insight: Globally optimal partition selection combined with entanglement-aware resynthesis can reduce quantum-circuit CNOT counts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports block-based circuit optimization with objectives such as minimizing partition count or weighted execution cost.
method: Enumerate qubit-feasible convex subcircuits.
Use integer linear programming to select partitions optimally over enumerated candidates and computed costs.
Resynthesize selected blocks using operator-Schmidt rank to exploit internal entanglement structure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 772 frozen local unitary targets, OSR yielded 741 verified syntheses versus BQSKit’s 617, matching or improving CNOT counts in all 617 jointly verified pairs.
infographic.watch_item: Optimality requires a proven-optimal ILP solution and is limited to enumerated candidates and computed costs; end-to-end comparisons also use different routing methods.
infographic.paper_title: Entanglement-Aware Quantum Circuit Optimization through Globally Optimal Partitioning

title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
authors: Teerawat Tongloy, Jiraporn Pongsopa, Rangsan Jomtarak
abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look more like the words annotators highlighted, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers on two short test pairs and kept or changed them under deletion as the model does; the evidence itself did not yet survive the device, and we work out the shots and calibration that measuring it on hardware would need.

infographic.key_insight: Born-measured attention enables exact finite-quadrature word evidence for class probabilities with input-fixed denominators, while matching a similarly sized softmax transformer on language inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic and qubit implementations, with a coherent attention layer requiring 23 qubits and 852 CNOTs.
method: Use row-normalized |⟨q|k⟩|⁴ attention, a measured-product nonlinearity, and Born readout.
Freeze denominators at input values to compute polynomial integrated-gradient evidence whose contributions sum correctly to within 10⁻¹¹ or better.
Test attention overlaps on IBM ibm_kingston using Hadamard tests.
infographic.evidence_signal: On e-SNLI, the model achieved 76.98 ± 0.17% accuracy versus 76.62 ± 0.36% for softmax; deleting its top-evidence word flipped 45% of predictions versus 32% for equivalently explained softmax.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware validation covered only two short test pairs: answers and deletion behavior matched, but word evidence did not survive device noise and needs further shots and calibration.
infographic.paper_title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits

title: Reasoning about Shared-Qubit Concurrency in Quantum Computing
authors: Mingsheng Ying
abstract: In this paper, we develop a semantic model for the parallel execution of quantum circuits, providing a formal foundation for studying shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing. As in classical shared-memory concurrency, parallel quantum circuits may interfere with one another through operations on shared qubits. However, quantum entanglement and the noncommutativity of quantum operations introduce additional challenges for reasoning about their correctness. To address these challenges, we generalise the classical Owicki-Gries method to quantum computing at the level of quantum circuits. Our approach enables compositional reasoning about parallel quantum circuits by separating the verification of individual components from the analysis of interference between them. We formulate proof rules for establishing the correctness of parallel quantum circuits and prove their soundness with respect to the proposed semantic model.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum generalisation of the Owicki–Gries method enables compositional correctness reasoning for parallel circuits that share qubits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides a formal basis for verifying shared-qubit parallel execution while accounting for entanglement and noncommuting operations.
method: Define a semantic model for parallel quantum circuit execution.
Separate component verification from shared-qubit interference analysis.
Formulate correctness proof rules and prove their soundness.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a soundness proof relative to the semantic model, but no empirical benchmarks or hardware evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical verification overhead and integration with quantum compilation workflows are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Reasoning about Shared-Qubit Concurrency in Quantum Computing

title: eigenkit: A Provider-Neutral Quantum Computing Library
authors: Laia Domingo, Daniil Tarpanov, Arsenii Senokosov, Asel Sagingalieva
abstract: Quantum software ecosystems provide increasingly capable tools for simulation and hardware execution, but differences in programming models, supported features, and backend capabilities can make it difficult to move and systematically compare the same quantum algorithm across execution environments. We introduce eigenkit, a provider-neutral quantum computing library that separates algorithm definition from backend execution through a common circuit representation and provider interface. The library currently supports 12 execution providers spanning simulators and quantum hardware, provides backend-independent gradient computation, and integrates with standard scientific-computing and machine-learning workflows through NumPy, PyTorch, and scikit-learn interfaces. We evaluate the practical relevance of this abstraction across both simulation and quantum hardware. Simulator performance varies substantially with circuit size, structure, batching, and application workload, showing that no single backend is consistently preferable. On quantum hardware, experiments on IBM Heron and IQM Emerald show that which processor is better suited to a given algorithm depends not only on hardware constraints, but also on how well the topology of the quantum algorithm matches the physical connectivity of the processor. These results demonstrate that backend portability is not only a software-design convenience, but can be important for both computational efficiency and quantum execution quality.

infographic.key_insight: eigenkit separates quantum algorithm definition from execution, enabling backend choice based on workload performance and hardware connectivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Provider-neutral circuits let engineers compare simulators and quantum processors without redefining algorithms for each backend.
method: Use a common circuit representation and interface across 12 execution providers.
Provide backend-independent gradient computation.
Integrate with NumPy, PyTorch, and scikit-learn workflows.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulator evaluations found no consistently preferable backend, while IBM Heron and IQM Emerald experiments showed that algorithm–hardware connectivity alignment affects execution quality.
infographic.watch_item: Portability does not guarantee equivalent performance or execution quality; backend capabilities and circuit topology still require evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: eigenkit: A Provider-Neutral Quantum Computing Library
